episodes.title: The New AI Agents That Shop, Plan, and Gossip
episodes.about: Will we have one AI assistant that does everything, or an entire network of agents that know different parts of our lives? David Pawlan, creator of Assistant Benchmark, returns with Anish Acharya and Josh Elman to take stock of how quickly the agent landscape has changed. David has now tested more than 140 AI assistants, and they unpack what separates them, from memory and judgment to trust, shopping, and social experiences. They also explore what happens when agents start talking to each other, how they could create new kinds of social networks and serendipity, and why the most compelling agents may ultimately do more than save time.
episodes.why: Out today: Pawlan has tested more than 140 AI assistants, and the useful split is not features but memory, judgment, and trust - plus what changes when agents start talking to each other instead of just to you.

episodes.title: AI Lurches Toward Recursive Self-Improvement
episodes.about: NLW's daily brief leads with recursive self-improvement: the accumulating signs that AI systems are starting to improve the process of building AI itself, and how close that loop is to closing. The episode works through the latest developments behind the claim and what a genuinely self-improving cycle would change about the pace of progress from here.
episodes.why: The lead claim is the big one: AI is starting to improve the process of building AI. NLW lays out the freshest evidence for that loop closing, and how much of it is real yet.

episodes.title: Can AI Invent or Just Help Scientists Work Faster? with Richard Socher - #783
episodes.about: AI can help scientists write code, analyze data, and draft papers. But can it generate the ideas that lead to new discoveries? Richard Socher, former chief scientist at Salesforce, founder of You.com, and co-founder of Recursive, joins to explore the move from AI assisting researchers to AI conducting research. Starting with AI improving AI, they examine what it takes to propose ideas, run experiments, and validate results, and how those capabilities could eventually accelerate discovery across biology, chemistry, and physics. The conversation covers Recursive's reported results in model training and GPU kernel optimization, why fast verification matters, and how reward hacking complicates the search for real improvements.
episodes.why: Socher draws the line that matters: writing code and drafting papers is assistance, but proposing the idea, running the experiment, and validating the result is invention - and he argues AI is crossing from the first to the second.

episodes.title: Will data centers rock the vote?
episodes.about: It's Election Day in the United States, and data centers have become a core issue in some of the country's most important midterm races. The Verge's Adi Robertson explains why people are uniting against data centers, why they've become a proxy for all kinds of other fights, and how this year's results might change the AI industry going forward.
episodes.why: Election Day made data centers a ballot issue: Robertson explains why neighbors are uniting against them, what they have become a proxy for, and how the midterms could reshape the AI buildout.

episodes.title: AI is changing mathematics -- but not how you think
episodes.about: Math has created some of humanity's oldest intellectual challenges, and AI is completely changing the game. This year AI solved one of math's most difficult problems. Since then, OpenAI has published hundreds of new math results. So is this the end for the people who've dedicated their careers to pushing forward math? NPR science correspondent Geoff Brumfel weighs the risks and rewards of AI's math takeover.
episodes.why: Discovery pick — Short Wave is NPR's daily science show, new here: 14 minutes on AI solving one of math's hardest problems and publishing hundreds of new results since, and what that does to the mathematicians.
